query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: A sufficient and optimized Al content in a CrFeCoNiAl alloy yields a slow-growing, adherent Al2O3 scale that acts as an effective diffusion barrier to both oxygen and metal cations, ensuring superior high-temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A CrFeCoNiAl high-entropy alloy prepared as a single-phase solid solution with homogeneous Al distribution.
generation.intervention: Compare CrFeCoNi alloys with Al versus those with non-Al X elements (e.g., Mn or Si) while maintaining similar processing conditions.
generation.conditions: Exposures above 900 °C in oxidizing and corrosive atmospheres, including environments containing chlorides.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an inner, dense and continuous Al2O3 layer that adheres strongly to the substrate, thereby reducing further oxygen ingress and metal cation outward diffusion.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum’s high oxygen affinity drives the formation of a thermodynamically stable, low-growth-rate alumina (Al2O3) scale. Provided that the Al concentration exceeds a critical threshold without causing detrimental depletion from the matrix, this scale limits diffusion, minimizes mismatch of thermal expansion, and resists cracking and spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The CrFeCoNiAl alloy will exhibit lower oxidation rates, more uniform oxide scale morphology, and improved mechanical integrity (fewer cracks/spalls) relative to CrFeCoNi alloys lacking adequate Al content.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNi alloys with X = Mn or Si that typically form faster-growing, less adherent oxide scales prone to cracking/spallation.
generation.boundary: Most effective when the alloy is maintained as a single-phase solid solution and when Al content is optimized to avoid depletion-induced embrittlement. Excessive Al could compromise mechanical properties if not balanced correctly.
generation.uncertainty: Although the protective nature of Al2O3 is well supported (see studies referenced in PMC9692591 and PMC11169556), the exact critical concentration for optimal alumina formation in complex high-entropy systems and its behavior under rapid thermal cycling remain partly uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one CrFeCoNiAl alloy with optimized Al content and one CrFeCoNi (non-Al) alloy using identical processing routes. Subject both sets to isothermal oxidation at 950 °C and thermal cycling conditions.
measurements: Utilize XRD and SEM to identify and analyze the oxide phases and morphology.
Perform weight gain measurements to monitor oxidation kinetics.
Conduct adhesion and bend tests to evaluate oxide scale integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not form a slow-growing, continuous Al2O3 scale with significantly improved oxidation resistance compared to the non-Al alloy, then the hypothesis is disproven.

cited_evidence.text: The Al oxide layer becomes a diffusion barrier to any other element(s) that is being oxidized, akin to colligative property (vapor pressure depression), as Al lowers the propensity of other elements to diffuse towards the oxidant. The Cr L-edge spectrum (Fig. 4e) shows a minor shift with the addition of Al to the HEA. Furthermore, the small change between unoxidized and oxidized states indicates that Cr2O3 forms rapidly upon exposure, indicating the likely immediate concomitant formation of both Al2O3 and Cr2O3 oxides. Mn L-edge spectrum (Fig. 4f), however, shows a change in the unoxidized condition with the addition of Al, where the oxidation state gets reduced to a lower state (Mn2+, forming MnO). This suggests a strong interaction between Al and Mn, as without Al, Mn initially oxidizes to Mn2O3 (Mn3+),, upon further oxidation, both alloys form the same oxide, MnO2 (Mn4+). The slower diffusing Fe shows a similar behavior to Mn where Al has an effect on to unoxidized state (Fig. 4g). Peaks shift from what was previously Fe3O4 (Fe2+/Fe3+) to Fe2O3 (Fe3+) again showing the strong interaction between Fe and Al.

cited_evidence.text: In the case of the Mn15Al5 alloy, the outer part of the oxide layer was mainly composed of Mn, suggesting the presence of MnxOy oxides followed by a thin layer of Cr-based oxides found at the metal/oxide interface. Moreover, a significant level of porosity was found within its closest proximity of it. The overall thickness of the whole layer after 100 h annealing reached approximately 25 µm. More importantly, the Mn15Al5 alloy was the only one showing strong sub-surface oxidation and developed internal porosity due to the diffusion of Mn toward the oxide layer. It was found that the sub-surface porosity reached up to ≈100 µm into the alloy core and likely may further progress with the increasing time of annealing. The present oxides within the metal were mainly composed of Mn and Al. Increasing the content of Al above 5 at.% resulted in a completely different behavior, forming a well-protective oxide layer containing foremostly Al, suggesting the formation of AlxOy without any traces of chipping or formation of sub-surface oxides.
